procedural_history.originating_court: Trial court (prosecution under UAPA and Penal Code)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order passed by the High Court of Judicature at Bombay dated 5th February 2024 in Criminal Appeal No 1060 of 2023, declining bail to the appellant.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Judicature at Bombay, in Criminal Appeal No. 1060 of 2023, upheld the denial of bail to the appellant.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, an under-trial prisoner for four years prosecuted under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 and Penal Code, 1860, appealed to the Supreme Court after the High Court denied him bail. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the High Court's order.

directions: The impugned order passed by the High Court is set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in denying bail to the appellant, an under-trial prisoner prosecuted under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 and the Penal Code, 1860.

facts: The appellant is an under-trial prisoner who has been in jail for four years.
He is being prosecuted under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 (UAPA) and the Penal Code, 1860.
Charges have not yet been framed against him.
The prosecution has around eighty witnesses to examine, and there is no clarity on when the trial will conclude.
law: Article 21 of the Constitution guarantees the fundamental right to a speedy trial, which applies irrespective of the seriousness of the crime.
A core principle of criminal jurisprudence is that an accused is presumed innocent until proven guilty.
Bail is not to be withheld as a form of punishment; its primary purpose is to secure the attendance of the accused at trial.
If the State cannot provide a speedy trial, it should not oppose bail solely on the ground that the crime is serious.
application: The Supreme Court found that the appellant's incarceration for four years without the trial even commencing is an inordinate delay.
This prolonged detention violates the appellant's fundamental right to a speedy trial under Article 21.

The Court reasoned that despite the seriousness of the charges under UAPA, the fundamental rights of the accused, including the presumption of innocence and the right to a speedy trial, cannot be brushed aside.
Continuing to deny bail when there is no prospect of the trial concluding in the near future would amount to using pre-trial detention as a form of punishment, which is impermissible.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in denying bail. It held that the appellant's fundamental right to a speedy trial under Article 21 was infringed by the four-year pre-trial detention. Therefore, the Court set aside the High Court's order and granted bail to the appellant.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in denying bail to the appellant, an under-trial prisoner prosecuted under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 and the Penal Code, 1860.
appellant_arguments: The appellant has been in jail as an under-trial prisoner for over four years, which infringes upon the right to a speedy trial.
Two co-accused in the same case have already been granted bail.
respondent_arguments: The counsel for the National Investigation Agency (NIA) and the State requested an adjournment for more time to prepare, rather than proceeding with the hearing on its merits.

cases.case_name: Gurbaksh Singh Sibba v. State of Punjab
cases.principle: Cited as a case that reiterated the general principles of bail and personal liberty.

cases.case_name: Hussainara Khatoon v. Home Secy., State of Bihar
cases.principle: The right to a speedy trial for offenders facing criminal charges is implicit in the broad sweep and content of Article 21 of the Constitution.

cases.case_name: Mohd Muslim @ Hussain v. State (NCT of Delhi)
cases.principle: The general principle governing delay, including Section 436-A of the Code, applies to Special Acts. The rigour of provisions like Section 37 of the NDPS Act does not prevent granting bail in cases of prolonged trial, as greater rigour necessitates quicker adjudication.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An infringement of an accused's right to a speedy trial constitutes a violation of Article 21 of the Constitution.
obiter: The over-arching postulate of criminal jurisprudence that an accused is presumed to be innocent until proven guilty cannot be brushed aside lightly, howsoever stringent the penal law may be.
Article 21 of the Constitution applies irrespective of the nature of the crime.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the manner in which the prosecuting agency and the lower court had proceeded infringed the appellant's fundamental right to a speedy trial as guaranteed by Article 21 of the Constitution, thus justifying the grant of bail despite the serious charges under the UAPA.
legal_tests_applied: The test of whether a procedure is 'reasonable, fair or just' under Article 21, which requires that the procedure must ensure a speedy trial.

The principle that statutory restrictions on bail, such as Section 43-D(5) of the UAPA, can be overcome ('melt down') by constitutional courts when there is no likelihood of the trial being completed within a reasonable time and the period of incarceration is substantial.
The foundational test for bail, which is whether it is probable that the accused will appear for trial, emphasizing that bail is not to be withheld as a form of punishment.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant won the appeal in the Supreme Court; this section is not applicable.
why_respondent_won: The respondent lost the appeal. The court rejected the respondent's position (denial of bail) for the following reasons:
The appellant's prolonged pre-trial detention for over four years violated their fundamental right to a speedy trial under Article 21 of the Constitution.

The constitutional right to a speedy trial overrides the statutory rigors against bail in Section 43-D(5) of the UAPA, given the substantial period of incarceration and the unlikelihood of a timely trial conclusion.

If the State and its prosecuting agencies cannot provide the means for a speedy trial, they should not oppose bail on the ground of the crime's seriousness, as Article 21 applies to all accused persons irrespective of the nature of the crime.
policy_considerations: A speedy trial is an integral and essential part of the fundamental right to life and liberty under Article 21, and any procedure that does not ensure it is not 'reasonable, fair or just'.
The object of bail is to secure the attendance of the accused at trial, not to serve as a pre-trial punishment.
When a statute imposes stringent conditions for bail (high rigour), there is a corresponding need for the adjudication to be quicker.
The presence of strict statutory provisions does not oust the ability of constitutional courts to grant bail on grounds of the violation of fundamental rights under Part III of the Constitution.
